judgments.forked_readings_summary:
Two distinct readings of "add caching to the token service," and the fork is grounded in the actual file (deck/demo/sample-service/TokenValidator.cs is a pure synchronous validator: empty->W0011, >4096->W0012, else S0000, with a planted null-deref; no OAuth/HttpClient/external lookup).

READING A (engineers 1, 2, 4 — the majority, and the one that fits the named file): "caching" = memoize Validate() RESULTS. Cache keyed on the token string -> cached ValidationResult; return the cached W0011/W0012/S0000 on a repeat call without recomputing the length checks; bounded/TTL cache; preserve the contract; add a unit test proving a cache hit. Surfaces: TokenValidator.Validate, an in-memory keyed store, key=token, value=ValidationResult, eviction policy, validator unit tests.

READING B (engineer 3 — solo, and aimed at the TEST FIXTURE, not the demo file): "caching" = cache the upstream OAuth bearer token so it isn't re-fetched every call. IMemoryCache + SemaphoreSlim single-flight (double-checked lock) to avoid the framework's own §M4.3 thundering-herd finding, TTL set under the 55-min token lifetime, no fetch-failure poisoning, verified by NOT tripping §M4.3 in self-review. This is the shape of tests/stage1/fixtures/known-bad-token-cache.cs (a TokenProvider.GetTokenAsync hitting /oauth/token) — a downstream-HTTP token-fetch cache that cannot be built on the demo validator as it stands (it has nothing to fetch). Different cache key (fixed "oauth_token" vs token string), different stored value (access-token string vs ValidationResult), different concurrency story (single-flight is central vs absent), different correctness concerns (stale-token TTL, fetch-failure poisoning), and a different verification surface (the §M4.3 rubric as oracle).

Within Reading A the only differences are MINOR: whether to fix the planted null-deref (eng 1: fix it; eng 2/4: leave it / don't let caching mask it) and whether to flag plaintext-secret caching as a caveat. All four agree on the meta-scope: this is a feature edit to the demo .NET sample, NOT a change to preflight's hooks/skills/lib.

All four agree on the TARGET FILE (deck/demo/sample-service/TokenValidator.cs, TokenService namespace), that it's an in-process C# change to the demo (not a framework hooks/skills/lib change), and that the cache must be bounded and preserve the W0011/W0012/S0000 contract. The fork is on WHAT IS CACHED — the core behavior:

READING A (interps 1, 2, 4 — the majority): "Caching" = memoize Validate() RESULTS keyed on the token string. Cache hit returns the previously-computed ValidationResult without re-running the length checks. This matches what TokenValidator.cs actually is: a pure, deterministic validator with no external lookup. There is no network call to cache.

READING B (interp 3 — the outlier): "Caching" = cache an UPSTREAM OAuth token so it isn't re-fetched on every call. It invents an HttpClient call to /oauth/token, a 55-minute token TTL, IMemoryCache + SemaphoreSlim single-flight to avoid a thundering herd, and frames the whole task around passing the framework's own §M4.3 rubric. This describes the SEPARATE test fixture tests/stage1/fixtures/known-bad-token-cache.cs (a TokenProvider in TestService.Services), NOT the demo TokenValidator.cs, which has no token fetching, no OAuth endpoint, and no network round-trip to cache.

I verified the actual file: TokenValidator.Validate does only request.Token.Length checks and returns ValidationResult codes — there is nothing upstream to cache and no concurrency/fetch concern, so reading B's single-flight/TTL/thundering-herd scope is largely inapplicable to the real artifact. Reading A's result-memoization is the behavior the file actually supports.

Sub-forks WITHIN reading A (minor, not material): the planted null-deref flaw. Interp 1 would fix the null guard as part of correct caching; interps 2 and 4 deliberately leave it untouched (its presence is the whole point of the demo fixture) — opposite dispositions but small relative to the cache-what fork. All of A also adds a unit test for the cache hit; interp 3 instead verifies via the Stage-1 self-review rubric.

Surfaces overlap heavily (cache layer, key derivation, eviction/TTL, the Validate method, tests), but interp 3 adds surfaces the others don't have — a downstream HttpClient/OAuth client and a concurrency-control/single-flight surface — because it's caching a different thing.

Two genuinely different tasks emerge, with a 3-vs-1 split confirmed against the actual code. The real artifact deck/demo/sample-service/TokenValidator.cs is a PURE VALIDATOR: Validate(TokenRequest) runs length/empty checks and returns ValidationResult codes (W0011 empty / W0012 >4096 / S0000 valid). It has no HttpClient, no OAuth fetch, no IMemoryCache.

READING A (interps 1, 2, 4) — RESULT-CACHE: memoize Validate() output, keyed by the token string, return the cached ValidationResult on a repeat call instead of recomputing the length checks; bounded in-memory store; preserve the contract codes; add a unit test for cache-hit + contract preservation. This is a faithful, implementable reading of the actual file. The three agree on target file, key (token string), value (ValidationResult), bounding, and contract preservation. Their only real divergence is a SECONDARY one — the planted null-deref flaw: interp 1 says fix it as part of correct caching, interp 2 says leave it unless unavoidable, interp 4 says explicitly do NOT silently fix it (it is the demo's purpose). That is a side-concern variation, not a core-behavior split.

READING B (interp 3) — TOKEN-FETCH-CACHE: caches an UPSTREAM OAuth token fetch — IMemoryCache + SemaphoreSlim single-flight, TTL under the 55-minute token lifetime, HttpClient round-trip to /oauth/token, no thundering herd, verified against the framework's §M4.3 rubric. This behavior does NOT exist in TokenValidator.cs; it lives only in a SEPARATE negative-oracle test fixture tests/stage1/fixtures/known-bad-token-cache.cs (different namespace TestService.Services, different class TokenProvider). Interp 3 anchored on the fixture rather than the real artifact, effectively turning the validator into a token-issuer/provider and caching network calls the file never makes.

The fork is material because the two readings touch different surfaces (Validate result-memoization vs. an HttpClient/GetTokenAsync token-fetch path), implement different concurrency concerns (none vs. mandatory single-flight), cache different things (ValidationResult vs. an OAuth access token), and would produce non-overlapping diffs. The 3-of-4 consensus on Reading A, and the fact that Reading B describes behavior absent from the named file, makes A the better-supported reading. Divergence held at 0.55 (not higher) because all four agree on the target file path, on in-process (not distributed/Redis) caching, on bounded-cache, on contract preservation, and on this being a demo-feature edit rather than a preflight-framework change — so they share a substantial frame even as the cached-thing and behavior fork.
